title: Quarnley Bar
passage:
Quarnley bar was a pole and a lamp at the top of a farm lane, three-quarters of a mile short of the Skelbrigg trust's main gate. It never paid for itself. In its best year it took less than the yearly wage of the tollman who sat there, and carts going about the two farms' business went through free, as the Act required. The lane climbed past the farms, forded the beck and rejoined the turnpike well beyond the main gate. In 1831 the trust's surveyor, Josiah Bardsell, put it to the board that the bar might stand unmanned until autumn. The board agreed, and the tollman spent the summer haymaking. Takings at the main gate fell that season by several times that wage, while the trust's other two gates took what they usually took. By September a man was back at Quarnley. Bardsell's report runs to a page and a half and does not mention the summer.
– Bryony Ombleby

questions.prompt: What does the text suggest about Quarnley bar?

options.text: That the traffic the trustees meant it to catch was the carting done by the two farms.
That it took too little to justify a tollman, and the board was right to do without it.
That leaving it unmanned cost the trust more at the main gate than the bar ever took.
That the bar had little to do with the fall in takings, which the season itself explains.

questions.rationale: TYPE-002, one_inch_inference. The text supplies three quantities and never puts them together. The bar's own receipts are small: 'It never paid for itself', and 'In its best year it took less than the yearly wage of the tollman who sat there'. When it stood unmanned, 'Takings at the main gate fell that season by several times that wage' - and the same sentence rules out a general slump, since 'the trust's other two gates took what they usually took'. The geography supplies the mechanism without stating it: the lane 'rejoined the turnpike well beyond the main gate', so a driver who took it missed the main gate altogether. Joining those gives C: the summer cost the trust, at a different gate, several times more than Quarnley bar had ever collected at its own. Nothing in the passage says this; the reader has to make the comparison, which is why the item is an inference rather than retrieval. A = scope-shift onto the wrong target: the two farms are the lane's most visible traffic and the trustees did put a bar where they carted, but the passage removes them from the bar's business in a single clause - 'carts going about the two farms' business went through free, as the Act required' - so the farms are precisely the traffic it was not there to catch. B = half-right conjunction, the most attractive of the three: its first half is straight from the text (the bar took less than a tollman's wage, and the board did agree to leave it unmanned), which lends the second half a borrowed credibility; but the second half is contradicted by what follows, since the main gate lost several times that wage and 'By September a man was back at Quarnley'. A reader who stops at the first clause selects it. D = the alternative-cause trap, aimed at the properly skeptical solver who knows that one bad season explains a great many falls in takings; the passage anticipates exactly that objection with its control - the trust's two other gates, in the same season and the same weather, 'took what they usually took' - so the season cannot carry the fall. Hedge balance: no option carries an absolutizer and none is the sole measured one, so neither 'pick the qualified answer' nor 'strip the absolutes' locates the key; the key runs 17 words against A 17, B 18 and D 17, so it is tied for second and is never the longest.
